NO. 441   PREMIUM EDITION   SUNDAY 29 MAY 2022

News



Snap’s slowdown 

Snap issued a profits warning ahead of the next quarter, saying that the macro environment was hitting it harder and faster than expected. It’s slowing hiring (though it will still add 10% this year) and looking for budget cuts. The stock almost halved, pulling Meta and others down as well. 

I am not an economist, but we are clearly still in the early stages of seeing how the macro environment will evolve (interest rates, supply chain, China, inflation, maybe food supplies, and more), how corporate and consumer spending will react to that, and what that means for advertising, ecommerce and corporate IT spending. Plus we don't know what else Apple will announce to destabilise advertising some more at WWDC next month. Expect volatility. RELEASE, STORY

Working out what the crash means for startups

One of the best books about bubbles and financial panics is called ‘This time it's different’ - and of course every bubble and every crash are indeed different. Today isn’t 2000 or 2008, for lots of reasons, but a decade of free money has ended, the hedge-fund tourists are going home, and valuations are down by at least half, which will cascade back down from public markets to the early stage. Entrepreneurs and VCs are pondering what this means, and obviously one of the first conclusions is that it’s a great opportunity for some content marketing. Here’s a sample. SEQUOIA, NFX, MERITECH, CRAFT

… and for local delivery

One hour local grocery delivery always looked like a top-of-the-market phenomena. Theoretically, you could make the algebra work with some level of competition, basket size and frequency at some levels of city density, but with multiple players burning capital to go for market share and hopefully to be the last man standing in a massively capital-intensive, low-margin market, this was always going to get painful once investors got sceptical and money stopped being free. Now they’re all slowing down and laying off. So who spent the money on building operational efficiency and who spent it on CAC? GORILLAS, ZAPP, GETIR

Amazon’s excess warehouses 

Amazon almost doubled its fulfilment square footage from 2019 to 2021, and it might (as the Silicon Valley saying goes) have got a little ahead of its skis. Now it’s looking at ending leases and subletting. LINK

A16Z doubles down on web3

A16Z’s crypto group announced a giant $4.5bn web3 fund. I don't generally do venture or funding news here, but this is interesting 1: as the last money out before the crash and 2: because the (presuming the standard 2&20) $90m of annual management fees on this will be spent on building software and tools to be released back into the community. The A16Z model has always been to use the fees to provide services to attract entrepreneurs, but actually making and publishing technology is new. (NB: I worked at a16z from 2014 to 2019.) LINK

… and we3

Meanwhile, a16z also led a round in Adam ‘Wework’ Neumann’s new venture, trading carbon credits on the blockchain. I don't really have an opinion on blockchain carbon trading, but a lot of people who did business with Adam Neumann have an opinion on him, and it’s all the same one. LINK

UK on Google adtech competition 

The UK’s CMA competition agency has a second investigation into Google’s advertising: last year it was the privacy sandbox; this year adtech. I’ve seen some people suggest that Google’s entire adtech/display business might or should be spun out. LINK

Twitter’s privacy screwup

Twitter has been fined $150m for pushing people to give them a phone number for 2FA and then using that number to target advertising, without notice or consent. This carried on until 2019. Oops. This is Elon Musk’s case for a change of management and culture. LINK

Xbox streaming dongle?

Microsoft is working on a cheap HDMI dongle (on the lines of a Chromecast) to act as an end point for the Xbox cloud streaming games service - to get it onto the TV. If and when streaming really works, the vision is to expand the number of people who would play (it removes the binary decision to buy a console or high-end phone), but I suspect shifting the business model and, much more, changing the kinds of games is more important. LINK

Apple reweights the supply chain

An ongoing story: Apple is trying to move more of its production outside China, due both to the short-term lockdowns and also to the longer-term political risk. The majority of the actual value in an iPhone has always come from outside of China (the chips from Taiwan, image sensors from Japan and so on) but the efficiency of massive scale final assembly is still concentrated in the Shenzhen cluster, and moving outside that is slow. LINK

Apple cars still smoking

CJ Moore, Tesla’s former head of cruise control (sorry, ‘Autopilot’) has left Apple’s car project for Luminar, a LIDAR company, following a great deal of other turnover on that team. It’s now apparently run by Kevin Lynch, who previously ran the Watch. 

There's not much one can say here, except that Apple has been working on this for a long time, some of the delay is probably around market timing (e.g. maturity of batteries and computer vision) and some of it is probably also about trying to work out what exactly they should be doing. LINK

Apple Glasses in June?

It appears that Apple has filed trademarks for ‘RealityOS’ with a deadline two days after its WWDC developer event on the 6th of June. Apple has never announced a flagship product at WWDC, but it did announce the iPhone before WWDC and started selling it after, and if it is launching an AR/MR/VR device it would want to help developers start building for it before it went on sale. After that, who knows? Has it solved the optics for actual glasses, or will it try to do a better Quest? And, of course, is this the next universal device after smartphones (as Meta believes) or a new accessory, like the Watch? LINK

Russia: still hacking

Google thinks that a new website of purportedly leaked emails from the UK Brexit campaign was set up by the Russian state. I would hope we’re wise to this pattern now. LINK

Google’s magic AI

After OpenAI’s DALLE earlier this year, Google now also has an amazing natural language image generation system, this one called Imagen. LINK

Gucci x Roblox

The fashion industry is doing a lot of experiments in web3, NFTs and metaverse, and this week Gucci is doing something in Roblox. This gives me painful memories of similar experiments in Second Life, although of course Second Life was a game without an actual game and Roblox is a lot more. LINK



Ideas



The WSJ reports on some of the people who were caught when Terra USD crashed, and lost their life savings, or worse. Key quote: “I thought it wasn't risky being in a stablecoin.” This is why financial regulation exists. LINK

An interesting piece on user studies inside UK government digital services. LINK

Rod Sims, the architect of Australia’s Link Tax fiasco, has published a self-justification which, unfortunately, doesn’t actually address the most substantive criticisms made of the policy. LINK

How do you address the discrepancy between the property taxes paid by physical stores in city centres and the much lower property taxes paid by fulfilment centres outside the city? Should there be an online sales tax? One of the U.K.'s biggest retailer says no, but it's an interesting fiscal policy question. LINK

Two pieces on Substack (a minority interest, I know): Vanity Fair on its content policies and the NY Times on financials and fund-raising (you can’t raise at 100x trailing revenue anymore). Lots of very round numbers in this, but if Substack has 1m paying subs and $9m net revenue, gross subs revenue is $90m, and ARPU is $90/year. At face value that implies very few people take more than one sub (and hence that it’s still not generating much discovery to support the 10% take rate)? VANITY FAIR, NYT

Meter, a new startup doing corporate wifi. The markets are collapsing, but meanwhile lots of people are out there founding companies that tackle some problem that already seemed solved, but with an idea for how to do it 10x better. LINK

Musicians are complaining about pressure from record labels to do lots of TikTok promotion. LINK

Brussels/USA privacy negotiations: still a mess. LINK

Meta has new terms of services, and they’re being released with a systematic and deliberate effort to handle this as customer comms, rather than letting the lawyers handle it. That’s an issue that’s caused big problems for all sorts of people in the past (including, recently, WhatsApp). Everything is marketing. LINK



Outside interests



San Francisco's latest biennial homelessness survey was released this month. 4,400 people are sleeping on the street (‘unsheltered’) on a typical night, down from 5,200 in 2019. In London, with almost exactly 10 times SF's population, the equivalent number (‘sleeping rough’) was 640 last year. Los Angeles Country, with roughly the same population as London, has 48,000. SF, LA, LONDON

The BBC has another big leak of data from China’s Uyghur concentration camps. LINK

Column



There's no such thing as data

Technology is full of narratives, but one of the loudest is around something called ‘data’. AI is the future, and it’s all about data, and data is the future, and we should own it and maybe be paid for it, and countries need data strategies and data sovereignty. Data is the new oil!

This is mostly nonsense. There is no such thing as ‘data’, it isn’t worth anything, and it doesn’t belong to you anyway.

Most obviously, ‘data’ is not one thing, but innumerable different collections of information, each of them specific to a particular application, that can't be used for anything else. Siemens has wind turbine telemetry and Transport for London has ticket swipes, and those aren’t interchangeable. You can’t use the turbine telemetry to plan a new bus route, and if you gave both sets of data to Google or Tencent, that wouldn’t help them build a better image recognition system. This might seem trivial put so bluntly, but it points to the uselessness of very common assertions, especially from people outside tech, on the lines of ’China has more data’ or ‘America will have more data’ - more of what data? Meituan delivers 50m restaurant orders a day, and that lets it build a more efficient routing algorithm, but you can’t use that for a missile guidance system. You can’t even use it to build restaurant delivery in London. ‘Data’ does not exist - there are merely many sets of data.

Of course, when people talk about ‘data’ they mostly mean your data - your personal information and the things that you do on the internet, some of which is sifted, aggregated and deployed by technology companies. We want more privacy controls, but we also think we should have ownership of that data, wherever it is.

The trouble is, most of the meaning in ‘your’ data is not in you but in all of the intersections with other people. What you post on Instagram means very little: the signal is in who liked your posts and what else they liked, in what you liked and who else liked it, and in who follows you, who else they follow and who follows them, and so-on outwards in a mesh of interactions between a billion people. If I like your picture, that is not your ‘my’ data or ‘your’ data alone, and it’s not worth anything without that context. You can't take that with you because you don't really own it (and certainly not in any binary sense), and even if you did you couldn’t plug it into TikTok, because TikTok has a different mesh and the users don’t overlap.

This prompted Tim O'Reilly to say that ‘data isn't oil - it's sand.’ Data is valuable only in the aggregate of millions. Indeed, this can be true even on a simple cashflow basis - in Q1 2022 Meta made just 99 cents of free cashflow per daily active user per month. This also applies even for data where you can meaningfully say that it’s ‘yours’. Your electricity usage is not about other people, but it’s not valuable by itself, only in the aggregate of all domestic electricity usage in south London or Brooklyn. And, again, data isn’t fungible - a power utility needs this data, but it’s no use to LinkedIn.

Indeed, for many of these systems the value isn't in the ‘data’ at all but in the flow of activity around it - the meaning is not in the picture or video you post but in how the network reacts to it tomorrow. You could see TikTok or PageRank as vast mechanical Turks - we do not yet have AI that can understand what every page, picture or video are in themselves, and so we need humans - all of us - in the loop somewhere, at the right point of leverage, liking, linking, clicking and watching. These are systems, not data, and the value is in the flow.

We’ve been here before: today’s AI looks a lot like databases in the 1980s. Both technologies transform what we can do with information and what questions we can ask, and how organisations can function. When databases were new, we worried, just as we do now about AI, and some of those worries were real, but no-one today asks if America has more database, or if it matters that SAP is German. No-one at Davos talks about ‘SQL colonialism’. These technologies are not strategic assets - anyone can have them, but what for? Databases enabled just-in-time supply chains, and Walmart, and let Apple make iPhones in China - those are the strategic questions. The same for AI, and ‘data’ - it’s not the new oil, just more software, so what do you build with it?
